title: Calvinism, made easy and complete
question: What is Calvinism, where did it come from, who shaped it, what good and harm has it done, and how do both sides read the Bible verses at the centre of the argument?
plainAnswer: Calvinism is a way of understanding salvation that puts God's choice first: people are so turned in on themselves by sin that none would turn to God unless God first chose them and changed their hearts, and God's choice does not depend on anything he foresaw in them. It is named after John Calvin (1509–1564), but its core ideas go back to Augustine in the 400s, and it was given its classic five-point shape at the Synod of Dort in 1618–19, long before the acronym TULIP was invented in the early twentieth century. Its admirers credit it with deep assurance, God-centred worship, schools, missions and ideas about limited government; its critics blame it for fatalism, anxious introspection, harshness and the execution of Michael Servetus. Both sides appeal to the Bible: non-Calvinists point to texts where God wants everyone saved and people resist him, Calvinists to texts where God chooses and draws. Most of the argument is not about whether these verses are inspired but about what words like 'all', 'world', 'draw' and 'choose' mean in context, and fair-minded believers have landed on both sides for sixteen centuries.
keyTakeaways: Calvinism's central claim is that salvation is God's work from start to finish: God chooses, Christ redeems, the Spirit renews, and the believer responds because God has first acted.

The ideas are older than Calvin: Augustine argued them against Pelagius around 411–430; Calvin systematised them; the Synod of Dort (1618–19) defined the 'five points'; the TULIP acronym dates only from about the early 1900s.

Calvinism is not fatalism and not 'hyper-Calvinism': mainstream Calvinists insist God works through means such as preaching, prayer and real human choices, and they offer the gospel freely to everyone.

Its legacy is mixed and argued over: assurance, worship, education, missions and political liberty on one side; Servetus, introspective anxiety, harshness, church splits and the debated use of Reformed theology to defend apartheid on the other.

The Bible debate turns on context and word meaning: 'all' and 'world' (1 Tim 2:4; 1 John 2:2), 'draw' (John 6:44; John 12:32), and whether Romans 9 and Ephesians 1 speak of individuals chosen for salvation or of groups chosen for a role.
Straw men abound on both sides: Calvinists do not think God is a puppeteer who doesn't care, and non-Calvinists do not think people save themselves.

sections.heading: What Calvinism is, in one breath
sections.body:
At its simplest, Calvinism answers one question: why does one person come to faith and another does not? The Calvinist answer is: because God, for reasons of his own and not because of anything better in the one who believes, chose to give that person a new heart. Faith is a gift (Eph 2:8-9), new birth comes from God and not from human will (John 1:12-13), and those God chose he will certainly bring to glory (Rom 8:29-30).

The main alternatives answer differently. Arminians (after Jacobus Arminius, 1560–1609) say God's grace goes before every person and makes faith possible, but each person can accept or resist it, and God chooses those he foresees will believe. Lutherans hold that God alone saves but that those who are lost reject grace by their own fault, and they refuse to reason further into the mystery. Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of 'synergy', human freedom cooperating with grace. Molinists try to combine strong sovereignty with free choice through God's 'middle knowledge'. 'Provisionists' (a recent label in Southern Baptist circles) hold that the gospel itself is God's sufficient means to enable any hearer to respond.

So the argument is not 'God's sovereignty versus human freedom' as if one side denied one of them. Every side believes in both. The disagreement is about how they fit together and which one explains the final difference between belief and unbelief.

callout.text: Myth: 'Calvinists believe in God's sovereignty; everyone else believes in free will.' In fact Arminians, Lutherans, Catholics and Orthodox all affirm God's sovereignty, and Calvinists affirm that people make real, willing choices. The dispute is over what kind of freedom humans have and what finally decides who believes.

sections.heading: The roots: Augustine versus Pelagius (c. 410–430)
sections.body:
Pelagius (c. 354–c. 418) was a British-born monk and moral teacher in Rome who was disgusted by lax Christians. He taught that God had given humans everything they needed to obey: Adam's sin set a bad example but did not corrupt human nature, so people could choose good without any special inner grace. His followers, such as Caelestius, pressed the point further.

Augustine of Hippo (354–430), the North African bishop whose *Confessions* tells how he could not free himself from his own desires until God changed him, saw this as a denial of the gospel. In a long series of writings he argued that since Adam all humanity is bound by sin, that the will is free to choose what it loves but cannot love God until grace heals it, that faith itself is God's gift, and that God has chosen some for salvation by sheer mercy. Late in life, in *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance* (c. 428–429), he taught that even perseverance to the end is a gift given to the elect.

The church sided with Augustine against Pelagius: a council at Carthage condemned Pelagian teaching in 418 and the Council of Ephesus confirmed the condemnation in 431. But it did not adopt all of Augustine. The Second Council of Orange (529) insisted that even the beginning of faith is grace, yet it also rejected any predestination to evil and said nothing about irresistible grace. Medieval theologians, Catholic and later Protestant, kept arguing over 'how much Augustine'. Calvinism is, in large part, one strong answer to that question.

sections.heading: John Calvin's life (1509–1564)
sections.body:
Profession: lawyer by training, then theologian, preacher, Bible commentator and pastor. Jean Cauvin was born on 10 July 1509 in Noyon, in Picardy, northern France, where his father worked as a legal and financial administrator for the local bishop. He was sent to Paris to study for the church, but his father, after a quarrel with the cathedral clergy, redirected him to law at Orléans and Bourges. There he also absorbed Renaissance humanism, the movement to go back to original sources; his first book (1532) was a commentary on the Roman philosopher Seneca.

Sometime around 1533–34 he was converted to the evangelical cause; he later described the change as sudden and as God subduing a stubborn mind. After his friend Nicolas Cop gave a reform-minded university address in Paris in November 1533, Calvin had to flee. In Basel in 1536 he published the first edition of the *Institutes of the Christian Religion*, a short handbook of Protestant belief with a preface defending persecuted French Protestants to King Francis I. He kept enlarging it until the final Latin edition of 1559 (French 1560).

Passing through Geneva in 1536, he was pressed by the reformer Guillaume Farel to stay. The city's council expelled both men in 1538 in a dispute over church discipline. Calvin spent three happy years in Strasbourg pastoring French refugees, learning from Martin Bucer and marrying Idelette de Bure (1540). Geneva invited him back in 1541, and he stayed until his death on 27 May 1564, preaching several times a week, writing commentaries on most of the Bible, setting up a consistory to oversee morals, founding the Geneva Academy (1559) and training pastors who carried Reformed faith into France, the Netherlands, Scotland and beyond. He was frequently ill, and his only child died in infancy; Idelette died in 1549.

Predestination was important to Calvin but not his organising centre: in the 1559 *Institutes* he placed it under the work of the Holy Spirit and the Christian life (Book 3), treating it as a comfort to believers rather than a starting axiom.

callout.text: Myth: 'Calvin ruled Geneva as a dictator.' Calvin was a pastor, not a magistrate; he did not become a citizen until 1559, and the city councils often overruled him. He had real moral influence, especially after 1555, but historians describe a negotiated, often tense relationship with the civil authorities rather than a theocracy run by one man.

sections.heading: The Servetus affair (1553), stated fairly
sections.body:
Michael Servetus (c. 1509/1511–1553) was a Spanish physician and scholar of real brilliance; he is credited with one of the first European descriptions of the blood's circulation through the lungs. He also rejected the doctrine of the Trinity and infant baptism, which in his century, for Catholics and Protestants alike, were crimes against the state as well as the church. He had corresponded angrily with Calvin for years. In 1553 he was arrested by Catholic authorities in Vienne, France, escaped, and was condemned and burned in effigy there.

In August 1553 he turned up in Geneva and was recognised at a sermon and arrested. Calvin supplied the theological charges and argued against him in the trial. The verdict and sentence belonged to Geneva's Small Council, which first consulted the Reformed churches of Zurich, Bern, Basel and Schaffhausen; all agreed he should be punished. He was burned alive at Champel on 27 October 1553. Calvin had asked that he be beheaded instead, a less cruel death, but the council refused.

Most Protestant leaders at the time, including the gentle Philip Melanchthon, approved. A minority did not: Sebastian Castellio published a protest in 1554 arguing that killing a man is not defending a doctrine. Calvin defended the execution in print. In 1903 Reformed Christians in Geneva erected an 'expiatory monument' at the site, honouring Calvin while condemning the error of his age. Both halves of the story matter: the execution was not unusual for the sixteenth century, and it was still a grave wrong that Calvin actively supported.

sections.heading: Theodore Beza and the Synod of Dort: where the 'five points' came from
sections.body:
Theodore Beza (1519–1605). Profession: lawyer, poet, then theologian, professor and Calvin's successor as leader of Geneva's pastors. Born at Vézelay in Burgundy, he studied law and wrote fashionable Latin poetry in Paris before a serious illness and conversion led him to Geneva in 1548. He taught Greek in Lausanne, became first rector of the Geneva Academy in 1559, defended the French Protestants at the Colloquy of Poissy (1561), published editions of the Greek New Testament, and led Geneva's church for four decades after 1564. Beza set out predestination in a more logical, system-like way (his 1555 chart of predestination is famous) and leaned toward 'supralapsarianism', the view that in God's plan the decree to elect comes logically before the decree to permit the fall. Historians debate whether this was a departure from Calvin or a natural development.

In the Netherlands, followers of the Leiden professor Jacobus Arminius issued the 'Remonstrance' of 1610: five articles teaching election based on foreseen faith, an atonement intended for all, the need for grace, grace that can be resisted, and uncertainty about whether true believers can fall away. The Dutch Reformed Church called an international synod at Dordrecht (Dort), November 1618 to May 1619, with delegates from Britain, the German territories and Switzerland. Its *Canons of Dort* answered the Remonstrants point by point under five 'heads of doctrine': unconditional election, an atonement effective for the elect, human corruption, effectual grace, and perseverance.

The synod's aftermath was harsh: some two hundred Remonstrant ministers were deposed, many exiled, and in a related political struggle the statesman Johan van Oldenbarnevelt was executed (May 1619) and Hugo Grotius imprisoned. The Remonstrants were tolerated again from the 1630s.

The word TULIP came much later. No sixteenth- or seventeenth-century writer used it, and its order does not even follow Dort's. The earliest known uses date from the early twentieth century in American Presbyterian circles; historian Kenneth Stewart traces it to around 1905–1913.

sources.author: Richard A. Muller
sources.title: Christ and the Decree: Christology and Predestination in Reformed Theology from Calvin to Perkins

callout.text: Myth: 'Calvin invented the five points of TULIP.' Calvin died in 1564; the five points come from the Synod of Dort's reply to the Remonstrants in 1619, and the TULIP acronym is an early-twentieth-century teaching device. Calvin's own views on the extent of the atonement are still debated by historians.

sections.heading: The Puritans and Jonathan Edwards
sections.body:
The Puritans were English (and later New English) Protestants who wanted the Church of England more fully reformed. Their theology was mostly Reformed, and they wrote some of its most searching pastoral literature. William Perkins (1558–1602), a Cambridge preacher and theologian, became the most-read English theologian of his generation and wrote at length on how a person can know they are elect. John Owen (1616–1683), Oxford vice-chancellor, chaplain to Oliver Cromwell and later a nonconformist pastor, wrote *The Death of Death in the Death of Christ* (1647), the classic defence of definite (limited) atonement, and still-loved works on sin and communion with God. The Westminster Assembly's Confession of Faith (1646–47) became the standard for Presbyterians worldwide. Not every Puritan was a strict Calvinist; Richard Baxter (1615–1691) held a moderate, more universal view of the atonement.

Jonathan Edwards (1703–1758). Profession: pastor, revival preacher, philosopher-theologian, missionary and briefly college president. Born in East Windsor, Connecticut, educated at Yale, he succeeded his grandfather Solomon Stoddard as pastor in Northampton, Massachusetts. Revivals broke out there in 1734–35 and again in the Great Awakening of 1740–42, when he worked alongside the English evangelist George Whitefield; his sermon 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' (1741) is famous, though most of his preaching dwelt on God's beauty. His *Religious Affections* (1746) tried to tell true conversion from emotional excess. Dismissed by his church in 1750 after a dispute over who could take communion, he became missionary pastor to Mohican and Mohawk people at Stockbridge, where he wrote *Freedom of the Will* (1754), arguing that people always choose according to their strongest desire, so they are free and responsible even though their choices are certain. He became president of the College of New Jersey (Princeton) in 1758 and died weeks later after a smallpox inoculation. He also owned enslaved people, which recent historians and admirers alike treat as a serious moral failure.

sections.heading: Princeton, Spurgeon and Lloyd-Jones
sections.body:
Charles Hodge (1797–1878). Profession: seminary professor and theologian. Born in Philadelphia, he taught at Princeton Theological Seminary for more than fifty years, training thousands of Presbyterian ministers. His three-volume *Systematic Theology* (1871–73) set out a confident, carefully argued Calvinism for the American church, and he edited the influential *Princeton Review*.

B. B. Warfield (1851–1921). Profession: seminary professor, theologian and New Testament scholar. Born near Lexington, Kentucky, he taught at Princeton from 1887 until his death. He is best known for defending the inspiration and inerrancy of Scripture and for *Counterfeit Miracles* (1918), the classic statement of cessationism, and he wrote widely on Calvin and Augustine. He spent much of his married life caring for his invalid wife, Annie, and was more open to some form of evolutionary biology than many later conservatives assume.

Charles Haddon Spurgeon (1834–1892). Profession: Baptist preacher, pastor, author and founder of institutions. Born in Kelvedon, Essex, he was converted at sixteen in a small Methodist chapel in a snowstorm, became pastor of New Park Street Chapel in London at nineteen and drew such crowds that the Metropolitan Tabernacle was built (1861). He never attended university, founded a Pastors' College and the Stockwell orphanage, and his sermons sold in their millions. Spurgeon was a convinced Calvinist who fought 'hyper-Calvinism' and pleaded with every hearer to come to Christ. He left the Baptist Union during the 'Downgrade Controversy' (1887–88) over what he saw as drift from biblical truth, and he lost American sales for preaching against slavery.

D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones (1899–1981). Profession: physician, then preacher and pastor. Born in Cardiff and raised in Wales, he trained at St Bartholomew's Hospital in London and became assistant to the royal physician Sir Thomas Horder before leaving medicine in 1927 to pastor a mission church in Aberavon, South Wales. From 1939 to 1968 he preached at Westminster Chapel in London, where his long expository series on Romans and Ephesians became classics. He helped revive interest in the Puritans (with the Banner of Truth publishing house), urged evangelicals in 1966 to leave doctrinally mixed denominations (a public disagreement with John Stott), and, unusually for a Calvinist, taught that a distinct baptism with the Spirit was available to believers.

callout.text: Myth: 'Calvinists don't evangelise.' Hyper-Calvinists such as some eighteenth-century English Baptists did hold that preachers should not urge the unconverted to believe. Mainstream Calvinists, from Whitefield and Spurgeon to Lloyd-Jones, rejected hyper-Calvinism and preached for conversions.

sections.heading: New Calvinism (from about 2000)
sections.body:
In the early 2000s a wave of younger American evangelicals, many of them Baptists or non-denominational, embraced Reformed theology. Journalist Collin Hansen called them 'Young, Restless, Reformed' in a 2006 *Christianity Today* article and 2008 book, and *Time* magazine listed 'the New Calvinism' among ideas changing the world in 2009. Networks such as The Gospel Coalition (founded 2005), Together for the Gospel and Desiring God gave it shape. It mixed Puritan-style doctrine with modern worship music, church planting and online teaching.

John Piper (born 1946). Profession: pastor, author and former biblical studies professor. Raised in South Carolina, he studied at Wheaton and Fuller and earned a doctorate in Munich, taught at Bethel College, then pastored Bethlehem Baptist Church in Minneapolis from 1980 to 2013. *Desiring God* (1986) taught 'Christian hedonism': God is most glorified in us when we are most satisfied in him. His ministry Desiring God is among the movement's most influential.

Timothy Keller (1950–2023). Profession: Presbyterian (PCA) pastor, church planter and apologist. From Allentown, Pennsylvania, he pastored in Virginia and taught at Westminster Theological Seminary before founding Redeemer Presbyterian Church in Manhattan in 1989, which grew among young urban professionals. *The Reason for God* (2008) became a bestseller; he co-founded The Gospel Coalition and helped plant hundreds of churches. He died of pancreatic cancer in May 2023.

R. C. Sproul (1939–2017). Profession: theologian, teacher, author and pastor. From Pittsburgh, he founded Ligonier Ministries in 1971, wrote *The Holiness of God* (1985) and *Chosen by God* (1986), and taught millions through radio and video. John MacArthur (1939–2025). Profession: pastor, Bible teacher and seminary president. Pastor of Grace Community Church in Sun Valley, California, from 1969, he founded The Master's Seminary and produced the *MacArthur Study Bible*. He combined Calvinist salvation teaching with dispensational views of prophecy and strong cessationism (*Strange Fire*, 2013), so he is better described as an elder ally of the movement than a 'New Calvinist' himself.

The movement has also faced criticism, including from inside: high-profile leadership failures (for example the collapse of Seattle's Mars Hill Church in 2014), disputes over complementarianism, and charges of tribalism. Supporters point to renewed seriousness about doctrine, preaching and church planting.

sections.heading: TULIP in plain words
sections.body:
T, Total depravity. Not 'everyone is as bad as possible', but 'sin has touched every part of us', mind, desires and will, so that left to ourselves we do not truly want God (Rom 3:10-12; Eph 2:1-3). People still do kind and admirable things; they simply cannot make themselves love God. Other traditions often agree with this point but add that God's grace already reaches out to everyone to free the will enough to respond.

U, Unconditional election. Before creation God chose particular people to save, not because he foresaw their faith or goodness, but out of his free mercy (Eph 1:4-5; Rom 9:11-16). Faith is the result of election, not its cause. The alternative ('conditional election') says God chose those he foreknew would believe (Rom 8:29; 1 Pet 1:1-2).

L, Limited atonement, which most Calvinists prefer to call 'definite' or 'particular redemption'. Christ's death was sufficient for all but intended to secure the salvation of the elect; he laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:11; Eph 5:25). Many Calvinists, the 'four-pointers' or 'Amyraldians', reject this point. Non-Calvinists hold Christ died for everyone (1 John 2:2).

I, Irresistible grace, better called 'effectual calling'. When God sets out to bring someone to new life, his Spirit does not fail; he changes the heart so that the person comes willingly (John 6:37; John 6:44). It does not mean people are dragged in against their will, nor that no one ever resists the Spirit for a time. The alternative says grace enables but can finally be refused (Acts 7:51).

P, Perseverance of the saints. Those God truly saves he keeps, and they will continue in faith to the end, not because they are strong but because he holds them (John 10:27-29; Phil 1:6). It is not 'once saved, always saved no matter how you live': Calvinists say real faith shows itself in a changed life. Arminians and Wesleyans hold that a true believer can fall away (Heb 6:4-6).

callout.text: Myth: 'Total depravity means people are incapable of any good.' Calvinist confessions affirm that unbelievers do many good things through God's common grace; the claim is that no part of human nature is untouched by sin and that no one, unaided, turns to God in faith.

sections.heading: Positive impacts, as adherents and many historians argue
sections.body:
Assurance and comfort. Calvin treated election as good news for anxious believers: if salvation rests on God's choice and not on our performance, it cannot be lost by our weakness (Rom 8:31-39). Many Calvinists testify that this gave them peace in suffering and persecution, from French Huguenots to modern believers.

God-centred worship and seriousness. Reformed churches stressed preaching through whole books of the Bible, psalm-singing, and a vision of all life lived 'to the glory of God' (1 Cor 10:31). Calvinism has produced a large literature of hymns, devotional writing and theology.

Education. Calvin's Geneva Academy (1559), the Scottish parish-school ideal, Dutch universities and early American colleges such as Harvard, Yale and Princeton drew on the Reformed conviction that every believer should read Scripture and that all knowledge belongs to God.

Missions. The modern Protestant mission movement owes much to Calvinists. William Carey (1761–1834), a Particular (Calvinistic) Baptist shoemaker-turned-pastor, wrote his *Enquiry* in 1792 and sailed for India the next year; his friend Andrew Fuller had argued that the gospel should be offered to all. David Brainerd, Henry Martyn and many Presbyterian and Dutch Reformed missionaries followed. Calvinists argue that confidence God has his people 'in every nation' fuels mission rather than killing it (Acts 18:9-10; Rev 7:9).

Political theory and work. Because Calvinists believed every ruler is under God and no human is sinless, many argued for limits on power: Beza's *Right of Magistrates* (1574), Samuel Rutherford's *Lex, Rex* (1644) and later Abraham Kuyper's idea of 'sphere sovereignty' (that family, church, state and school each have their own God-given authority). Some historians link these ideas to constitutional government and resistance to tyranny. The sociologist Max Weber famously proposed in 1904–05 that a Puritan 'work ethic', partly driven by the search for signs of election, helped give rise to modern capitalism; that thesis remains contested and many economic historians reject it in its strong form.

callout.text: Often-told story: when young William Carey proposed foreign mission at a ministers' meeting, an older minister told him to sit down because God would convert the heathen without his help. The story comes from later family recollections and its wording is uncertain; even if it happened, Carey's own Calvinist circle went on to found the Baptist Missionary Society.

sections.heading: Negative impacts, as critics argue
sections.body:
Fatalism. Critics say that if God has settled everything, prayer, evangelism and moral effort lose their point. Calvinists answer that God ordains means as well as ends, so prayer and preaching are the very ways his plan comes about (Westminster Confession 3.1 and 5.2), and that fatalism is a misunderstanding; the hyper-Calvinist minority who stopped inviting sinners proves the danger is real, though.

Assurance anxiety. Ironically, a doctrine meant to comfort could also torment. Later Puritan writers taught believers to examine their lives for evidence of election, and some fell into deep doubt about whether they were among the chosen. Historian R. T. Kendall argued (1979) that this came from a shift between Calvin and later Calvinists; others, such as Paul Helm, dispute that reading. Ex-Calvinists today often report similar fears.

Harshness and the Servetus legacy. Critics point to Servetus, to strict church discipline in Geneva and Scotland, and to a reputation for severity and joylessness. Defenders reply that other confessions were no gentler and that Reformed piety has also produced deep warmth and joy.

Apartheid theology, debated. In South Africa, leaders of the Dutch Reformed Church (NGK) gave theological backing to racial separation, drawing on ideas of distinct peoples and spheres associated with neo-Calvinism. Historians debate how far this was Calvinism and how far nationalism using Christian language. It was also Reformed Christians who led the opposition: Beyers Naudé, Allan Boesak and others; the World Alliance of Reformed Churches declared apartheid a heresy in 1982, and the Belhar Confession (1982, adopted 1986) rejected it on Reformed grounds.

Church splits and tribalism. The Synod of Dort ended with Remonstrant pastors deposed; George Whitefield and John Wesley split over predestination in the 1740s; many Presbyterian and Baptist bodies divided over these questions; and recent Southern Baptist life has seen bitter disputes. Critics say Calvinism breeds argument and pride in doctrinal precision; Calvinists reply that clarity about the gospel is worth contending for, while admitting that some adherents have been needlessly combative.

sections.heading: The verses Calvinists rely on: Romans 9
sections.body:
Romans 9 is the chapter both sides know best. Paul is grieving that most of Israel has not believed in Jesus and asks whether God's word has failed (Rom 9:1-6). He answers that not all descended from Israel are 'Israel': God chose Isaac, not Ishmael, and Jacob, not Esau, before the twins were born or had done good or bad, so that God's purpose in election might stand, not because of works but because of him who calls (Rom 9:6-13). God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills (Rom 9:18). When someone objects, 'then why does he still blame us?', Paul answers with the image of a potter who has the right to make vessels for honour and for dishonour (Rom 9:19-23).

The Calvinist reading: Paul is explaining why some individuals believe and others do not, and his answer is God's free choice. The objections Paul anticipates ('is God unjust?' 9:14; 'who can resist his will?' 9:19) only arise if he is teaching unconditional election; if election were based on foreseen faith, the obvious answer would be 'no, God chose those who would believe', which Paul never gives. Corporate groups are made of individuals. Key defenders: Augustine, Calvin, John Piper (*The Justification of God*, 1983), Thomas Schreiner.

The non-Calvinist readings: (1) Corporate and historical: Jacob and Esau stand for nations (Gen 25:23; Mal 1:2-3), and Paul is explaining God's freedom to choose which people carry his purposes in history, now including Gentiles, not who goes to heaven. (2) The point of the chapter is that God can define his people by faith rather than ancestry, which is exactly where Paul ends (Rom 9:30-32; Rom 10:9-13). (3) The potter image comes from Jeremiah 18:1-10, where the potter reshapes a nation according to how it responds. (4) Paul says God 'prepared beforehand' the vessels of mercy, but the vessels of wrath are described with a verb many read as 'fitted' or 'ready' for destruction, perhaps by their own doing (Rom 9:22-23). (5) Romans 9 must be read with Romans 11, where hardened Israelites can be grafted back in if they do not continue in unbelief (Rom 11:23) and God has consigned all to disobedience in order to have mercy on all (Rom 11:32).

sections.heading: Ephesians 1, John 6, Acts 13:48 and other Calvinist texts
sections.body:
Ephesians 1:4-11. God 'chose us in him before the foundation of the world' and 'predestined us for adoption', according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will. Calvinist reading: particular people were chosen before time, by God's will alone, and the purpose is unshakeable (Eph 1:11). Non-Calvinist reading: the key phrase is 'in him'. God chose Christ, and chose a people in Christ, the way Israel was chosen in Jacob; individuals come to share that election when they are joined to Christ by faith (Eph 1:13 'when you believed'). What is predestined is the goal (adoption, holiness), not who believes. Some Arminians instead tie election to foreknowledge (Rom 8:29; 1 Pet 1:2).

John 6:37-44 and 6:65. All the Father gives Jesus will come to him; no one can come unless the Father draws him, 'and I will raise him up on the last day'. Calvinist reading: those drawn are the same ones raised, so drawing does not fail; it is effectual and given to the elect only. Non-Calvinist readings: verse 45 explains the drawing as hearing and learning from the Father, i.e. through his teaching, which can be resisted; John 12:32 says Jesus will draw 'all people', so drawing is necessary but not by itself decisive (Wesley's 'prevenient grace'); some read 'those the Father gives' as faithful Israelites who already trusted the Father and were handed to Jesus.

Acts 13:48. When Gentiles in Pisidian Antioch heard the gospel, 'as many as were appointed to eternal life believed'. Calvinist reading: the appointment came first; faith followed. Non-Calvinist reading: the Greek participle could be read as middle voice, 'as many as were disposed (or lined up) for eternal life', contrasting with the Jewish listeners who 'judged themselves unworthy' (Acts 13:46). Most translations keep 'appointed' or 'ordained'.

Other texts Calvinists cite: John 10:26 ('you do not believe because you are not my sheep', not the other way round); Rom 8:29-30 (the 'golden chain' in which all the foreknown are glorified); Eph 2:1-9 (dead people cannot raise themselves; salvation is God's gift; both sides agree the 'gift' in 2:8 refers to the whole package of salvation by grace through faith); Phil 1:29 (it has been granted to you to believe); John 1:12-13 (born not of human will but of God). Non-Calvinists reply that 'foreknew' in Rom 8:29 implies God knew something about them, that John 10:26 describes settled unbelievers rather than the never-elect, and that 'dead' in Eph 2 is a picture of separation, not total inability.

sections.heading: Straw men on both sides, corrected
sections.body:
About Calvinists. 'They believe God creates people just to damn them.' Mainstream Calvinists say every person who is lost is lost for their own sin, and God takes no pleasure in it (Ezek 33:11); they treat reprobation (God passing over some) as a mystery they speak of reluctantly. 'They think we are robots.' Calvinists hold that people choose freely in the sense that they do what they most want; they deny only that the fallen will can, unaided, want God. 'They don't care about evangelism.' See Whitefield, Carey, Spurgeon and the modern church-planting networks. 'Calvinists think they are better than others.' The doctrine teaches that the elect were chosen despite having nothing better about them (Deut 7:7-8; 1 Cor 1:26-29), though individual pride is a real risk they themselves warn against.

About non-Calvinists. 'They think people save themselves.' Arminians and others teach that no one can believe without prior grace and that faith earns nothing. 'They deny God's sovereignty or foreknowledge.' Classical Arminians, Molinists and others affirm God's complete foreknowledge and sovereign rule; only the small 'open theism' movement denies exhaustive foreknowledge, and most Arminians reject it. 'They make God the servant of human choices.' Their claim is that God sovereignly chose to create free creatures and to save those who trust him; that, they argue, is itself a sovereign decision. 'They believe you can lose your salvation every time you sin.' Wesleyans and Arminians who hold that believers can fall away usually mean deliberate, persistent rejection of Christ, not ordinary failures.

On both sides, the most respected writers agree that the other side are brothers and sisters in Christ. Wesley and Whitefield disagreed sharply but Wesley preached at Whitefield's funeral; Spurgeon called Wesley a saint while disputing his theology.

table.caption: Scripture by scripture: verses often raised against Calvinism, the Calvinist reply, and the non-Calvinist counter-reply
rows: John 3:16
God loves 'the world' and promises life to 'whoever believes'; that sounds universal and open to all.
'World' stresses the size and unworthiness of what God loves (people of every nation, sinful humanity); 'whoever believes' says who is saved, not who is able to believe (John 6:44).
In John 3:17 and John 1:29 'world' is humanity at large; an offer to 'whoever' is empty if most hearers cannot respond; John 3:19 blames refusal, not lack of election.
1 Tim 2:4
God 'desires all people to be saved' and come to the truth.
Either 'all kinds of people' (the context mentions kings and rulers, 2:1-2) or a real desire of God's revealed will that he does not decree to fulfil for wise reasons ('two wills' in God).
Verse 1 says pray for all people and verse 6 says Christ gave himself as a ransom for all; a God who decrees against what he desires is hard to make sense of.
2 Pet 3:9
God is not willing that any should perish but that all should reach repentance.
Peter writes to 'you', the beloved; God delays judgment until all his chosen ones are gathered (John Owen). Others use the 'two wills' answer.
The letter's readers are a mixed group and the verse explains God's patience toward the world; 3:15 says his patience means salvation, which is natural if it is for all.
1 John 2:2
Christ is the atoning sacrifice for the sins of the whole world.
'Whole world' means not only Jewish believers but people from every nation (compare John 11:51-52); Christ's death is sufficient for all but applied to the elect.
John uses 'the whole world' in 5:19 for all people under the evil one; nothing in the context limits it; many four-point Calvinists agree the atonement is universal in some sense.
Ezek 18:23
God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but in their turning.
True: God does not delight in death as such; he ordains judgment for wider purposes while grieving over sin, as a judge can sentence without pleasure.
If God could give a new heart to every sinner and chooses not to, his 'no pleasure' rings hollow.
Ezek 33:11
'Turn, turn ... why will you die?' implies the hearers really can turn.
Commands show duty, not ability (Luther against Erasmus); God uses the command itself as the means by which he gives life to the elect (Ezek 36:26-27).
'Why will you die?' locates the cause of death in the hearers' choice; Ezek 18:31 tells them to make themselves a new heart.
Matt 23:37
Jesus longed to gather Jerusalem but 'you were not willing'; his will was resisted.
It is Jerusalem's leaders who refused while Jesus wanted to gather 'your children'; or it expresses God's revealed desire, not his decree.
Separating leaders from children is strained; the lament makes most sense if the refusal was real and not decreed.
Heb 2:9
Jesus tasted death 'for everyone'.
The context defines 'everyone': the 'many sons' brought to glory, his 'brothers', the 'children' God gave him (Heb 2:10-13).
'Everyone' is naturally universal, and Heb 2:14 grounds it in Christ sharing the flesh and blood of all humanity.
God is 'the Saviour of all people, especially of those who believe'.
'Saviour' here means preserver and benefactor of all (common grace), and Saviour in the full sense of believers; some read 'especially' as 'namely'.
The verse fits an atonement provided for all and applied to believers far more naturally than a two-sense reading.
Titus 2:11
God's grace has appeared bringing salvation to all people.
'All people' means all kinds of people; the preceding verses address older men, women, the young and slaves (Titus 2:1-10).
Grace that 'brings salvation to all' fits the idea of grace that reaches everyone and enables a response (prevenient grace).
Acts 7:51
'You always resist the Holy Spirit': the Spirit can be resisted.
Calvinists agree people resist the Spirit's outward call; the inward, effectual call overcomes resistance (Canons of Dort 3/4).
If the Spirit can be resisted, the decisive difference lies in the human response; the two-calls distinction is not in the text.
People 'enlightened' who 'shared in the Holy Spirit' can fall away.
They had real but non-saving experience of the Spirit's work; the writer expects 'better things' of true believers (Heb 6:9); or the warning is God's means of keeping the elect.
The descriptions are of genuine believers; the warning only works if falling away is a real possibility.
God consigned all to disobedience to have mercy on all.
'All' means Jews and Gentiles as groups, the subject of Romans 11, not every individual.
The 'all' who disobeyed and the 'all' who receive mercy match; the scope is as wide as sin.
Deut 30:19
'Choose life': a choice set before everyone presupposes ability.
Calvinists affirm real, willing choices; the problem is the heart's desire, and the same speech says God must circumcise hearts (Deut 29:4; Deut 30:6).
Moses calls the choice 'not too hard' (Deut 30:11-14), which Paul applies to the gospel (Rom 10:6-8).
John 12:32
Jesus will 'draw all people' to himself.
'All people' means Gentiles as well as Jews (Greeks have just come, John 12:20-21); the same verb in John 6:44 is effectual, so a universal effectual drawing would mean universalism.
Exactly: since not all are saved, drawing must be resistible; John 6:44 says drawing is needed, John 12:32 says it is given to all.
2 Pet 2:1
False teachers deny 'the Master who bought them', so Christ bought some who perish.
'Bought' may echo Deut 32:6 (God as owner-creator) or describe what the teachers claimed, not saving redemption.
'Bought' is redemption language elsewhere (1 Cor 6:20; Rev 5:9); the plain sense counts against definite atonement.
'Whoever wishes, let him take the water of life freely.'
Calvinists preach this free offer to everyone; whoever comes will be welcomed (John 6:37); grace makes people thirsty.
A sincere universal offer sits awkwardly with an atonement made only for some and a grace given only to some.
Isa 55:1
'Everyone who thirsts, come': a universal invitation.
Same answer: the invitation is genuine and universal; those who come prove that God has worked in them.
The invitation names the condition (thirst), not a secret election; Isa 55:7 calls 'the wicked' to return.
Luke 7:30
The Pharisees 'rejected the purpose of God for themselves'.
'Purpose' here is God's revealed counsel calling them to repent, not his secret decree (which cannot be thwarted, Eph 1:11).
Luke shows God's saving purpose for particular people can be refused.
God provides 'the way of escape' so believers can resist temptation; real alternatives exist.
Written to believers; God gives both the way out and the will to take it (Phil 2:13); real choices are compatible with God's ordaining.
If God decrees whether we take the way out, his provision of it seems theatrical.
Jas 1:13
God tempts no one; if he ordains everything, he ordains sin.
God ordains all things but is not the author of sin (Westminster Confession 3.1); sin comes from our desires (Jas 1:14); Gen 50:20 shows God meaning for good what humans meant for evil.
Critics such as Roger Olson find 'ordains but is not the author' a verbal distinction that does not remove the problem.
Rom 2:4
God's kindness is meant to lead people to repentance, including those who do not repent.
God's kindness is a real call to all; only effectual grace turns the call into repentance.
If God's kindness is 'meant' to lead them to repentance, his intention for them was salvation.
Acts 17:30
God 'commands all people everywhere to repent'.
The command is universal and sincere; ability is a separate question (Ezek 36:26-27).
A command to all reflects God's will for all; Paul goes on to say God appointed a day to judge the world by Christ (Acts 17:31).

title: 'Jesus is perfect theology' and the hard texts of the Old Testament
question: If Jesus shows us exactly what God is like, how should Christians read Old Testament stories where God commands war, sends fire or strikes people dead?
plainAnswer: All Christians agree that Jesus is the clearest window onto God (John 14:9; Heb 1:3). They disagree about what to do when an older text seems to show God acting unlike Jesus. Cruciform or christocentric readers (such as Greg Boyd, Brian Zahnd and Peter Enns) say the cross is the lens: where an Old Testament portrait of God clashes with the self-giving love of Jesus, it reflects the limited view of its human writers, or God stooping to work through them, rather than God's true character. Whole-canon readers (such as Paul Copan, Matthew Flannagan and most Reformed theologians) say every part of Scripture truly reveals God, that judgment was just and often described with wartime exaggeration, and that Jesus himself speaks as judge. A middle, christotelic view reads the whole story as moving toward Jesus, so older texts are true but partial and find their full meaning in him, without being written off. Each view has to answer a hard question: the first must avoid sliding into the second-century heresy of Marcion, who rejected the Old Testament God; the second must explain how commands to destroy whole peoples fit a God who is love; the third must show how it differs in practice from either.
keyTakeaways: 'Jesus is perfect theology' is a phrase popularised by Bill Johnson of Bethel Church, mostly about God's will to heal and do good; others have applied the same instinct to Old Testament violence.

Cruciform readers let the cross 'filter' Old Testament portraits of God; whole-canon readers let all of Scripture, including Jesus as judge, define God together; christotelic readers see the Old Testament as true but partial, completed in Christ.

Jesus' rebuke of James and John when they wanted to call down fire like Elijah (Luke 9:54-55) is the parade example for cruciform readers; whole-canon readers note Jesus does not condemn Elijah, and that the longer wording in some Bibles is a later manuscript addition.

Copan and Flannagan argue that conquest language such as 'leave nothing alive' is stock ancient war hyperbole, since the same books say the peoples remained; critics reply this softens but does not remove the problem.
The New Testament also contains severe judgment (Ananias and Sapphira; Revelation 19), so a simple 'Old Testament angry God, New Testament loving God' contrast does not fit any of the three views.
The church rejected Marcion's two-gods teaching; no mainstream party today accepts it, and accusing cruciform readers of being Marcionites is a charge they explicitly deny.

sections.heading: Where the phrase comes from
sections.body:
Bill Johnson (born 1951) is senior leader of Bethel Church in Redding, California, a large charismatic congregation known for its worship music and its school of supernatural ministry. He has long used the phrase 'Jesus Christ is perfect theology' in sermons and writing. In his use the main point is practical: if you want to know God's will about sickness, oppression or hopelessness, look at Jesus, who healed all who came to him and never refused anyone (Matt 4:23-24; Acts 10:38). So, he argues, Christians should not explain away suffering as God's will when Jesus consistently opposed it.

The phrase rests on texts all Christians accept: whoever has seen Jesus has seen the Father (John 14:9); the Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact imprint of his nature (Heb 1:3); he is the image of the invisible God (Col 1:15); in former times God spoke in many ways through prophets, but now through his Son (Heb 1:1-2). The disagreement is not about whether Jesus reveals God perfectly but about what follows for reading the rest of the Bible.

Others, especially Greg Boyd and Brian Zahnd, have applied a similar conviction ('God is like Jesus') to the Old Testament's violent portraits of God. It is fairer not to assume that everyone who uses Johnson's phrase holds Boyd's or Zahnd's full view, or vice versa. Critics of Johnson's own use usually focus on healing: they argue that Jesus' perfection as revelation does not mean every believer will be healed now (2 Cor 12:7-9; 2 Tim 4:20).

sources.author: Brian Zahnd
sources.title: Sinners in the Hands of a Loving God

callout.text: Myth: 'People who say Jesus is perfect theology think the rest of the Bible doesn't matter.' Bill Johnson, Greg Boyd and Brian Zahnd all affirm the whole Bible as inspired Scripture. Their claim is about which part interprets which, not about cutting texts out.

sections.heading: The cruciform (christocentric) view in plain words
sections.body:
The word 'cruciform' means 'cross-shaped'. Greg Boyd (born 1957), a pastor in Minnesota and former theology professor, sets out the fullest version in *The Crucifixion of the Warrior God* (2017, with a shorter popular version, *Cross Vision*). His argument runs like this. The cross is God's supreme self-revelation: God shows who he is by suffering for his enemies rather than destroying them (Rom 5:8-10; 1 John 4:8-10). So any portrait of God must be read 'through' the cross. When an Old Testament text shows God commanding the slaughter of children, that portrait reflects the fallen and culturally limited view of the human author. Yet God really did inspire the text: just as on the cross Jesus allowed himself to be pictured as a cursed criminal (Gal 3:13), God humbly allowed his people to picture him in violent ways, bearing their sin in the way they portrayed him. Boyd also argues that in many judgment stories God 'withdraws' his protection and lets sin and destructive forces take their course (Rom 1:24-28), rather than acting violently himself.

Brian Zahnd (born 1959), pastor of Word of Life Church in Missouri, makes a similar case in pastoral, popular form. Peter Enns (born 1961), a biblical scholar, frames it as the Bible being an ancient, human library in which Israel told its story of God in the categories of its time; Jesus and the apostles then reread that story creatively. Eric Seibert's *Disturbing Divine Behavior* (2009) distinguishes the 'textual God' from the 'actual God'.

The main supports they cite: Jesus overturns 'eye for an eye' and 'hate your enemy' with love of enemies, because that is what the Father is like (Matt 5:38-48); Jesus refuses to call down fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:51-56); Jesus says Moses permitted divorce 'because of your hardness of heart' (Mark 10:5), showing that some Old Testament laws were accommodations rather than God's ideal.

sections.heading: The whole-canon view in plain words
sections.body:
Whole-canon readers (critics sometimes call this a 'flat' reading, a label they reject) hold that every part of Scripture reveals God truly, though not every part equally fully. The God who judged Canaan is the God revealed in Jesus. Three main arguments are offered.

First, judgment is just. God waited centuries until the sin of the Amorites was 'complete' (Gen 15:16); Canaan is described as practising child sacrifice and other evils (Lev 18:21-25; Deut 12:31); Israel itself was later judged by the same standard (Lev 18:28; 2 Kgs 17:7-18). As Creator and giver of life, God has the right to end it, and all humans are under the sentence of death for sin (Rom 6:23). On this view the cross does not cancel wrath; it is where wrath and mercy meet (Rom 3:25-26).

Second, the language is often hyperbole. Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan, in *Did God Really Command Genocide?* (2014), argue that phrases like 'utterly destroy' and 'leave nothing that breathes' were standard exaggerations in ancient Near Eastern war reports, meaning 'win decisively'. They point out that after Joshua is said to have destroyed everyone (Josh 10:40; Josh 11:16-23), Judges records the same peoples still living there (Judg 1:21-36), and the main command elsewhere is to 'drive out' the inhabitants (Exod 23:28-30; Num 33:52). The targets were chiefly military strongholds, the episode was limited to one time and place, and it was never a model for later wars.

Third, Jesus himself affirms the Old Testament and speaks as judge. He says Scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35), refers to the flood and Sodom as real judgments (Luke 17:26-30), warns of hell more than anyone in the New Testament (Matt 10:28), and is pictured returning in judgment (2 Thess 1:7-9; Rev 19:11-16). So 'Jesus is perfect theology' cuts both ways: the perfect revelation of God includes his holiness and judgment. Reformed theologians, from Augustine and Calvin to Clay Jones, hold versions of this view.

sources.author: Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan
sources.title: Did God Really Command Genocide? Coming to Terms with the Justice of God

callout.text: Myth: 'Whole-canon readers enjoy violence or think God is cruel.' Copan, Flannagan, Christopher Wright and others write precisely because they find these texts troubling. They argue that judgment is a grievous necessity God undertakes reluctantly (Ezek 33:11; Lam 3:33), not that violence is good.

sections.heading: The middle way: christotelic, progressive revelation
sections.body:
'Christotelic' means 'with Christ as the goal (telos)'. The term was popularised by Peter Enns in *Inspiration and Incarnation* (2005), though Enns has since moved closer to the cruciform view. Others in this broad middle include Richard Hays, Christopher J. H. Wright, Brevard Childs and Graeme Goldsworthy, with roots in Irenaeus' second-century idea that God educated humanity step by step.

The idea is that the Bible is one unfolding story, and later chapters shed light on earlier ones the way the end of a novel makes you reread the beginning (Luke 24:27; Luke 24:44-47). Earlier revelation is true, not mistaken, but partial: it belongs to a particular moment in God's dealing with a particular nation. Jesus fulfils, deepens and sometimes reconfigures what came before ('you have heard it said ... but I say', Matt 5:21-48), and he explains some laws as concessions to hardness of heart (Mark 10:5). So readers should not take a conquest command as a model for Christians today, nor should they decide the text was wrong about God.

Christopher Wright, for example, says frankly that he cannot fully explain the conquest, but places it within the larger story: it was a limited act of judgment, the same God later judged Israel, God's purpose was always to bless all nations (Gen 12:3), and the story ends at the cross where God takes judgment on himself and at the new creation where the nations are healed (Rev 22:2).

Critics from the cruciform side say this leaves God still commanding the killing of children; critics from the whole-canon side worry that 'reconfiguring' can become a way of quietly setting texts aside. Christotelic writers reply that holding tension honestly is better than resolving it too quickly either way.

sources.author: Richard B. Hays
sources.title: Reading Backwards: Figural Christology and the Fourfold Gospel Witness

sections.heading: Example 1: Elijah's fire and James and John (2 Kgs 1; Luke 9:54-55)
sections.body:
In 2 Kings 1 King Ahaziah sends soldiers to arrest Elijah; twice Elijah calls down fire from heaven and fifty men die; the third captain pleads for mercy and is spared (2 Kgs 1:9-15). Centuries later, when a Samaritan village refuses to welcome Jesus, James and John ask whether they should call down fire to consume them, and Jesus turns and rebukes them (Luke 9:51-56).

A textual note matters here. Some later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add that the disciples said 'as Elijah did' and that Jesus said they did not know what spirit they were of, for the Son of Man came not to destroy lives but to save them. The earliest manuscripts lack these words, so most modern translations put them in a footnote. Luke's text simply says Jesus rebuked them.

Cruciform reading: Jesus explicitly refuses the Elijah model; the spirit of Christ does not destroy enemies, so the Elijah story shows a prophet acting in a pre-Christ spirit. Whole-canon reading: Jesus rebukes the disciples' vengeful zeal toward people who merely failed to show hospitality, at a time when his mission was to save, but he never says Elijah or God was wrong, and in Luke 4:25-26 and James 5:17-18 Elijah is honoured. Christotelic reading: the episode shows that in Christ the time of mercy has come, and disciples must not take up prophetic fire as their own weapon, while the final judgment belongs to God alone (Rom 12:19).

sources.author: Bruce M. Metzger
sources.title: A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament

callout.text: Whichever view you hold, check your Bible's footnote at Luke 9:55: the best-known line about 'what spirit you are of' is probably not original to Luke, though it is an ancient addition and faithfully reflects the sense of Jesus' rebuke.

sections.heading: Example 2: the conquest of Canaan
sections.body:
The commands to devote the Canaanite peoples 'to destruction' (Hebrew *herem*) are the hardest case (Deut 7:1-5; Deut 20:16-18; Josh 6:21; 1 Sam 15:3). The texts give reasons: the land's own sins, the danger that Israel would adopt child sacrifice and idolatry, and God's ownership of the land (Deut 9:4-5; Deut 18:9-12; Lev 25:23).

Cruciform readers say a God who commands the killing of infants cannot be the God who gave himself for his enemies; the commands record Israel's sincerely held but limited perception of God, which God allowed and bore. Whole-canon readers answer with justice (centuries of patience, Gen 15:16), hyperbole (the same peoples survive, Judg 1), limited scope (only these nations at this time, Deut 20:10-15 treats distant cities differently), and God's sovereign right over life. Christotelic readers place the conquest within a story moving from judgment on Canaan, to judgment on Israel, to the cross, while noting that Rahab the Canaanite was spared and even entered the line of Jesus (Josh 6:25; Matt 1:5).

One point unites most interpreters today: these commands are not a pattern for Christians. The New Testament directs believers' warfare against spiritual powers, not people (Eph 6:12; 2 Cor 10:3-4).

sources.author: Stanley N. Gundry (ed.)
sources.title: Show Them No Mercy: Four Views on God and Canaanite Genocide

sections.heading: Example 3: Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:1-11)
sections.body:
In the early Jerusalem church a couple sell land and pretend to give all the proceeds while keeping some back. Peter tells Ananias he has lied not to people but to God, and Ananias falls down dead; three hours later Sapphira repeats the lie and dies too, and 'great fear' comes on the church (Acts 5:1-11).

This story matters because it is in the New Testament, after Pentecost. It tests every view. Cruciform readers note that the text never says God struck them; it reports that they fell down and died, and some suggest the shock of exposure or the destructive power of sin itself, with Peter announcing rather than causing the outcome. Whole-canon readers say this shows the same holy God in both Testaments: the church, as God's new temple, is protected as the tabernacle was (compare Nadab and Abihu, Lev 10:1-2, and Achan, Josh 7), so there is no 'violent Old Testament God versus gentle New Testament God'. Christotelic readers see a founding-moment sign, like the Old Testament parallels, rather than a pattern for church discipline, and note that the church's normal response to sin is restoration (Gal 6:1; 2 Cor 2:5-8).

Whatever view one takes, the story undercuts the popular idea that the Bible's two halves show two different moods of God.

callout.text: Myth: 'The Old Testament God is wrathful; the New Testament God is loving.' The Old Testament describes God as merciful, gracious and slow to anger (Exod 34:6-7; Jonah 4:2), and the New Testament contains Ananias and Sapphira, Herod's death (Acts 12:23) and Revelation's judgments. None of the three views in this guide holds the simple contrast.

sections.heading: The Marcion question
sections.body:
Marcion of Sinope (c. 85–c. 160), a wealthy shipowner who joined the church at Rome, taught that the Creator God of the Old Testament, a God of law and justice, was a different and lesser being from the good Father revealed by Jesus. He rejected the Old Testament and accepted only an edited Gospel of Luke and ten letters of Paul. The Roman church expelled him around 144, and writers such as Irenaeus and Tertullian (*Against Marcion*, c. 207–208) answered him at length: the God who created is the God who redeems, and the Old Testament is Christian Scripture. Marcion's challenge pushed the church to clarify its canon.

Whole-canon critics sometimes say that cruciform readers are 'functional Marcionites': not teaching two gods, but in practice treating large parts of the Old Testament as untrue about God. Cruciform writers reject the charge firmly. Boyd, for example, insists that the Old Testament is fully inspired and that the 'warrior God' passages are themselves revelation, read through the cross; the difference from Marcion, he argues, is that he keeps every text and one God. Christotelic writers sit between, warning both against Marcion's rejection and against ignoring the progress of revelation.

It is fair to say that no one in this debate teaches Marcion's two gods. The live question is narrower: can a reader say that a text's portrait of God is inaccurate in some respects while still calling that text God's inspired word?

sources.author: Judith M. Lieu
sources.title: Marcion and the Making of a Heretic

callout.text: Whether cruciform hermeneutics drifts toward Marcionism is itself a central point of the debate. Critics see a pattern of setting texts aside; defenders see a faithful way of letting the clearest revelation interpret the less clear.

sections.heading: What difference it makes, and straw men to avoid
sections.body:
In preaching, cruciform readers tend to preach Old Testament violence as a mirror of human projection that the cross exposes and overturns. Whole-canon readers preach it as a sobering picture of God's holiness and judgment that drives us to the cross where judgment is borne. Christotelic readers preach it as a stage in a story that culminates in Christ. In prayer and ministry, Bill Johnson's version of the phrase leads to confident prayer for healing; critics urge that confidence be paired with acceptance when healing does not come.

All three views agree on more than they sometimes admit: Jesus is the fullest revelation of God; the Old Testament is Christian Scripture; Christians must not use these texts to justify violence; and God's final word is mercy and new creation for his people.

Straw men to avoid. Not every cruciform reader is a liberal who denies inspiration; Boyd and Zahnd write as evangelical or charismatic pastors. Not every whole-canon reader is untroubled by these texts; many write with evident anguish. And christotelic readers are not simply fence-sitters; they hold a principled view of how stories and revelation develop.

title: Have the miraculous gifts stopped? Cessationism and continuationism explained
question: Did gifts like prophecy, tongues and healing end with the apostles, or should churches expect them today?
plainAnswer: Cessationists believe the 'sign' gifts, such as prophecy, tongues and miracles of healing, were given to confirm the apostles and lay the foundation of the church, and stopped once that foundation and the New Testament were complete; God still heals and guides, but not through people who hold those gifts. Continuationists believe every gift in the New Testament remains available until Christ returns, and that the church should eagerly seek them while testing them carefully. Between them, an 'open but cautious' view accepts that the gifts may continue but is wary of many modern claims. The church fathers reported such gifts into the second and third centuries, later writers such as John Chrysostom noted they had become rare, B. B. Warfield made the classic cessationist case in 1918, and the Pentecostal and charismatic movements since 1906 have made continuationism the experience of hundreds of millions. The key text, 1 Corinthians 13:8-10, says gifts will cease 'when the perfect comes', and most scholars on both sides now think that means the return of Christ.
keyTakeaways: Everyone agrees the Holy Spirit lives in every believer and gives gifts today; the question is about specific gifts: prophecy, tongues, interpretation, healings and miracles.

Cessationists' strongest arguments are the foundational role of apostles and prophets (Eph 2:20), the confirming purpose of signs (Heb 2:3-4), the sufficiency of completed Scripture, and the gap between New Testament gifts and many modern claims.

Continuationists' strongest arguments are that no text says the gifts end before Christ returns (1 Cor 1:7; 1 Cor 13:12), that Paul commands believers to seek them (1 Cor 14:1; 1 Cor 14:39), and widespread testimony past and present.
'When the perfect comes' (1 Cor 13:10) is read by most commentators, including leading cessationists such as Richard Gaffin, as the return of Christ; cessationism usually rests on other arguments.
The history is mixed: early fathers report gifts, later fathers note their rarity, Augustine changed his mind, and the modern Pentecostal movement began at Topeka (1901) and Azusa Street (1906).
In practice, churches differ in worship style, how they seek guidance, how they pray for the sick, and what they treat as authoritative.

sections.heading: The words in plain English
sections.body:
Cessationism (from 'cease') holds that certain gifts ceased with the apostolic age. Continuationism holds that all the gifts continue. 'Open but cautious' is a middle label for those who see no biblical reason the gifts must have stopped but are hesitant about most modern practice.

The gifts in question are mostly listed in 1 Corinthians 12:8-10: words of wisdom and knowledge, special faith, gifts of healing, working of miracles, prophecy (speaking a message prompted by God), distinguishing spirits, speaking in tongues (languages the speaker has not learned, whether human or heavenly) and interpreting tongues. Other lists (Rom 12:6-8; Eph 4:11; 1 Pet 4:10-11) include teaching, serving, giving, leading and mercy, which no one thinks have ceased.

Three continuationist streams are worth knowing. Pentecostals (from 1901–06) usually teach a 'baptism in the Spirit' after conversion, often evidenced by tongues. Charismatics (from about 1960) brought these gifts into existing Protestant and Catholic churches, often without the 'evidence' doctrine. The 'Third Wave' (1980s, associated with John Wimber and the Vineyard) emphasised signs and wonders in evangelical churches while treating Spirit-baptism as part of conversion.

callout.text: Myth: 'Cessationists don't believe in miracles.' Cessationists believe God still answers prayer and can heal miraculously. What they deny is that people today hold the gifts of miracles, healing or authoritative prophecy as the apostles did.

sections.heading: What the New Testament shows
sections.body:
On the day of Pentecost the disciples spoke in other languages, and Peter explained it from Joel: in the last days God will pour out his Spirit on all flesh, sons and daughters will prophesy, and the promise is for 'you and your children and for all who are far off' (Acts 2:1-18; Acts 2:38-39). Tongues, prophecy and healing recur through Acts (Acts 10:44-46; Acts 19:6; Acts 21:9; Acts 28:8-9).

Paul spends three chapters on the gifts (1 Cor 12-14). He says the Corinthians lack no gift as they wait for the revealing of Christ (1 Cor 1:7), urges them to pursue love and earnestly desire spiritual gifts, especially prophecy (1 Cor 14:1), and closes with 'do not forbid speaking in tongues' (1 Cor 14:39). He also regulates them strictly: two or three speakers, interpretation required, prophecies weighed (1 Cor 14:27-33). Elsewhere he says not to despise prophecies but test everything (1 Thess 5:19-21).

Other texts point toward a special, foundational role. The church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Eph 2:20). Signs, wonders and miracles are called 'the signs of an apostle' (2 Cor 12:12). Hebrews says the message was confirmed to us by those who heard the Lord, with God bearing witness by signs and gifts (Heb 2:3-4), using a past tense. In the later letters Paul leaves Trophimus ill (2 Tim 4:20) and advises Timothy to take wine for his stomach (1 Tim 5:23).

The longer ending of Mark (Mark 16:17-18), which promises signs including tongues and healing, is missing from the earliest manuscripts and is widely regarded as a later addition, so both sides usually avoid resting weight on it.

sections.heading: What the church fathers reported
sections.body:
Second-century writers speak of the gifts as still present. Justin Martyr (c. 100–c. 165), a philosopher-convert teaching in Rome, told a Jewish debater that prophetic gifts remained among Christians in his day (*Dialogue with Trypho* 82). Irenaeus of Lyon (c. 130–c. 202) wrote that he had heard of believers who spoke in all kinds of languages through the Spirit and that some had even seen the dead raised (*Against Heresies* 2.32.4; 5.6.1). Origen in the third century said traces of the Spirit's power still remained among Christians, driving out demons and healing (*Against Celsus* 1.46).

The Montanist movement (from about 156–172 in Phrygia), whose prophets claimed new revelations and ecstatic speech, made church leaders more wary of prophecy. The church did not reject prophecy as such, but it increasingly tied authority to bishops and the apostolic writings.

By the late fourth century some leading writers describe the gifts as past. John Chrysostom, preaching on 1 Corinthians 12 in Antioch around 390, said the passage was obscure because the things it describes used to occur but no longer do (*Homilies on 1 Corinthians* 29). Augustine at first said tongues had ceased because they were a sign for the first age (*Homilies on 1 John* 6.10), but later, after recording healings in his own diocese at Hippo connected with the relics of Stephen, he described many contemporary miracles (*City of God* 22.8) and qualified his earlier statement (*Retractations* 1.13).

Cessationists read this pattern as decline after the apostolic age; continuationists read it as evidence of continuation, with fluctuations tied to the spiritual health and institutional shape of the church.

callout.text: Both sides claim the fathers. A fair summary is that clear reports of gifts continue into the third century, that by the late fourth century major writers considered the apostolic-style gifts rare or past, and that miracle reports (especially around saints and relics) never disappeared.

sections.heading: From the Reformation to Warfield
sections.body:
In the Middle Ages miracle stories clustered around saints, shrines and relics. Protestant Reformers, arguing with Catholic critics who said the new churches lacked miracles to confirm them, replied that the gospel had already been confirmed by the apostolic miracles; they were suspicious of contemporary miracle claims as props for doctrines they rejected. Calvin, for example, argued in his preface to the *Institutes* that the Reformers preached no new gospel needing new miracles. Yet some Reformed figures were credited with prophetic foresight (for example the Scottish reformers George Wishart and John Knox in later accounts), and John Wesley in the eighteenth century was open to continuing gifts.

The classic modern cessationist case came from B. B. Warfield (1851–1921) of Princeton Seminary in *Counterfeit Miracles* (1918). He argued that miraculous gifts were the credentials of the apostles, passed on only through the apostles' laying on of hands (Acts 8:14-18), and so died out with the generation they touched; he then examined later miracle claims, from patristic to Catholic to faith-healing movements, and found them wanting. Modern cessationists such as Richard Gaffin (*Perspectives on Pentecost*, 1979), O. Palmer Robertson, Thomas Schreiner and John MacArthur (*Strange Fire*, 2013) argue less from Warfield's history and more from the foundational, revelatory nature of prophecy and tongues and the closing of the canon.

sections.heading: Azusa Street and the charismatic renewal
sections.body:
On 1 January 1901 at Charles Parham's Bible school in Topeka, Kansas, student Agnes Ozman spoke in tongues after prayer, and Parham taught that tongues were the evidence of Spirit-baptism. In 1906 William J. Seymour, an African American holiness preacher who had studied under Parham, led a revival in a former church building at 312 Azusa Street in Los Angeles. It ran almost daily for about three years, drew people of many races (remarkable in segregated America), and sent missionaries worldwide. Denominations such as the Assemblies of God (1914) and the Church of God in Christ grew from this movement.

In 1960 the Episcopal priest Dennis Bennett in Van Nuys, California, announced he had spoken in tongues, marking the start of the charismatic renewal within older churches. The Catholic charismatic renewal began at a retreat for Duquesne University students in 1967. In the 1980s John Wimber's Vineyard movement and the 'Third Wave', a name used by C. Peter Wagner, brought healing prayer and prophecy into broadly evangelical churches.

Today Pentecostal and charismatic Christians are among the fastest-growing parts of world Christianity, especially in Africa, Latin America and Asia. A widely cited 2011 Pew Research Center estimate put them at about 584 million people, roughly a quarter of all Christians. Many testimonies of healing and deliverance come from these regions; scholar Craig Keener collected and analysed such reports in *Miracles* (2011).

sections.heading: 1 Corinthians 13:8-10: 'when the perfect comes'
sections.body:
Paul writes that love never ends, but prophecies will pass away, tongues will cease and knowledge will pass away; for we know in part and prophesy in part, but when the perfect (or 'complete', Greek *to teleion*) comes, the partial will pass away. Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face; now I know in part, then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known (1 Cor 13:8-12).

Three readings. (1) The perfect is the completed New Testament canon: once Scripture was finished, partial revelation ceased. This was popular in some twentieth-century cessationist writing but is now held by few scholars, because 'face to face' and 'know fully as I am known' sound like the end of history, not the closing of a book. (2) The perfect is the church's maturity, as in Eph 4:13; a minority view. (3) The perfect is the return of Christ and the new creation. Most commentators hold this, including continuationists such as Gordon Fee and many cessationists such as Richard Gaffin.

So this text, on the majority reading, says the gifts will end at Christ's return; it does not settle whether they also faded earlier. Cessationists who accept reading (3) usually rest their case on Ephesians 2:20, Hebrews 2:3-4 and the nature of revelation, not on this verse. Continuationists argue that reading (3) at least makes it natural to expect the gifts throughout the church age.

callout.text: Myth: 'Cessationism depends on reading the perfect as the Bible.' Many leading cessationists agree the perfect is Christ's return. Their argument is that the gifts' purpose was foundational, not that this verse announces their end.

sections.heading: The strongest arguments each way
sections.body:
Cessationist case at its best. (1) Foundation: apostles and prophets laid the church's foundation once (Eph 2:20); you do not keep laying a foundation. (2) Purpose: signs confirmed the apostolic message (Heb 2:3-4; 2 Cor 12:12; Mark 16:20) and that confirmation has been given. (3) Scripture's sufficiency: if New Testament prophecy was the very word of God, ongoing prophecy would add to Scripture, which is complete (Jude 1:3; 2 Tim 3:16-17). (4) Quality gap: New Testament healings were instant, total and public, including the lame walking and the dead raised; many modern claims, they argue, are partial, private or unverified. (5) History: miracles in the Bible cluster around Moses, Elijah and Elisha, and Jesus and the apostles, rather than being constant. (6) Pastoral safety: claims of new revelation have often led to manipulation or false teaching.

Continuationist case at its best. (1) No stopping point: Paul expects the gifts until Christ is revealed (1 Cor 1:7; 1 Cor 13:10-12), and Peter's promise extends to 'all who are far off' (Acts 2:39). (2) Commands: believers are told to desire prophecy and not forbid tongues (1 Cor 14:1; 1 Cor 14:39); these instructions were not marked as temporary. (3) Two kinds of prophecy: Wayne Grudem and others argue that ordinary congregational prophecy was always to be weighed (1 Cor 14:29; 1 Thess 5:20-21) and so never had the authority of Scripture; it adds nothing to the canon. (4) Gifts served more than confirmation: they build up the church (1 Cor 12:7; 1 Cor 14:3-4) and that need continues. (5) Testimony: church history and global Christianity today contain many credible reports. (6) Consistency: if God still heals in answer to prayer, why should he not do so through gifted people?

The open-but-cautious view (D. A. Carson's *Showing the Spirit*, 1987; J. I. Packer's *Keep in Step with the Spirit*, 1984; Robert Saucy) agrees there is no clear exegetical case for cessation but doubts that most modern phenomena match the New Testament, and stresses love, order and the centrality of Scripture.

sections.heading: Practical differences in church life
sections.body:
Worship services. Continuationist churches often leave room for spontaneous prayer, prophetic words, tongues with interpretation, and extended singing; cessationist churches tend toward a structured service centred on preaching and prescribed prayers. Many open-but-cautious churches allow such gifts in small groups but not on Sunday.

Guidance. Continuationists may expect God to speak through impressions, dreams or prophetic words, always tested by Scripture. Cessationists stress that God guides through Scripture, wisdom, counsel and providence, and are wary of 'God told me' language.

Prayer for the sick. Both pray for healing and both may anoint with oil (Jas 5:14-16). Continuationists more often pray with expectation of immediate healing and lay on hands publicly; cessationists more often pray for healing 'if it is God's will', alongside medical care. Both, at their best, care for those who are not healed.

Deliverance. Continuationists frequently practise prayer to expel evil spirits; cessationists generally believe in demonic activity but approach it through ordinary pastoral care, prayer and Scripture.

Risks each side names. Continuationists warn cessationists of 'quenching the Spirit' (1 Thess 5:19) and of a faith that expects little from God. Cessationists warn continuationists of false prophecy, manipulation, financial exploitation and damage when promised healings do not come. Responsible leaders on both sides acknowledge these risks in their own camp.
